title: How much oxalic acid is in a rust remover?

stimulus.title: Titrating a rust remover
stimulus.text:
A powdered rust remover contains oxalic acid, H₂C₂O₄ (molar mass 90.04 g/mol), mixed with substances that do not react with bases. Oxalic acid is a weak acid, present in water mostly as H₂C₂O₄ molecules. In the titration each molecule gives up both of its acidic protons to hydroxide ions, forming the oxalate ion, C₂O₄²⁻.

A student weighs 1.2500 g of the powder, dissolves it in distilled water and makes the solution up to exactly 250.0 mL. She titrates 25.00 mL portions of this solution with 0.1045 M NaOH, using phenolphthalein as the indicator.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe how the student should prepare the 250.0 mL of solution from the weighed powder. Name the glassware.

rubric.point: Names a 250.0 mL (250 mL) volumetric flask for making up the solution.
accept: transfer to a 250 mL volumetric flask

rubric.point: Describes dissolving the solid in less than 250 mL of water, transferring it all (rinsing the beaker into the flask), then adding distilled water to the calibration mark and mixing.
accept: dilute to the mark and invert to mix
rinse the beaker into the flask, fill to the line, stopper and invert

parts.sample: Dissolve the 1.2500 g of powder in about 100 mL of distilled water in a beaker, then pour it into a 250.0 mL volumetric flask. Rinse the beaker several times with distilled water and add the rinsings to the flask so no acid is lost. Add distilled water until the bottom of the meniscus is on the calibration mark, then stopper and invert the flask several times to mix.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the average volume of NaOH used.

rubric.point: Volumes 23.76, 23.71 and 23.72 mL; average 23.73 mL (four significant figures).

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the mass percent of oxalic acid in the powder. Show your setup.

rubric.point: Uses the 1 : 2 mole ratio and scales from the 25.00 mL portion to the whole 250.0 mL: 0.002480 ÷ 2 = 0.001240 mol per portion; × 10 = 0.01240 mol in the sample.
Mass percent: 0.01240 mol × 90.04 g/mol = 1.116 g; 1.116 g ÷ 1.2500 g × 100 = 89.3% (consistent with earlier steps, with a reasonable number of significant figures).

parts.sample: Moles OH⁻ = 0.1045 mol/L × 0.02373 L = 0.002480 mol. Moles H₂C₂O₄ in 25.00 mL = 0.002480 mol × (1 mol H₂C₂O₄ / 2 mol OH⁻) = 0.001240 mol. The 25.00 mL portion is one tenth of the 250.0 mL, so the sample held 0.01240 mol. Mass = 0.01240 mol × 90.04 g/mol = 1.116 g. Mass percent = 1.116 g ÷ 1.2500 g × 100 = 89.3%.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the reaction between oxalic acid and sodium hydroxide in the titration, and identify the Brønsted-Lowry base in it.

rubric.point: Writes H₂C₂O₄(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → C₂O₄²⁻(aq) + 2H₂O(l), with oxalic acid as a molecule (weak acid), Na⁺ omitted as a spectator and atoms and charge balanced, AND identifies OH⁻ as the base (proton acceptor).

parts.sample: H₂C₂O₄(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → C₂O₄²⁻(aq) + 2H₂O(l). Oxalic acid is weak, so it is written as molecules; Na⁺ is a spectator. Charge is −2 on each side. OH⁻ is the Brønsted-Lowry base, because it accepts the protons given up by oxalic acid.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: The student rinsed the buret with distilled water but did not rinse it with the NaOH solution before filling it. Predict whether the calculated mass percent of oxalic acid is too high, too low or unchanged, and justify your answer.

rubric.point: Justifies: water in the buret dilutes the NaOH, so a larger volume is needed to deliver the moles that react; the calculation uses 0.1045 M with the larger volume, overstating moles of NaOH, so moles and mass of acid come out too large.
accept: diluted titrant needs more mL, and more mL × the label molarity gives too many moles

parts.sample: Too high. Water left in the buret dilutes the NaOH, so its real concentration is below 0.1045 M and more volume is needed to react with the same moles of acid. The calculation multiplies the label concentration, 0.1045 M, by this larger volume, so it counts more moles of NaOH than were used, giving too many moles of oxalic acid and a mass percent that is too high.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: Another student says the 25.00 mL portions should be titrated in dry flasks, because water in the flask would change the result. Explain why this is not necessary.

rubric.point: Explains that water in the flask does not change the moles of oxalic acid in the 25.00 mL portion, and the NaOH needed depends only on those moles.
accept: extra water changes concentration, not moles of acid

parts.sample: The 25.00 mL pipetted into the flask contains a fixed number of moles of oxalic acid. Extra water dilutes it but does not change the moles, and the volume of NaOH needed depends only on the moles of acid, so a wet flask gives the same result.
